summary: FullSleep Navigator is an interactive lunar south-pole explorer that turns a location and a date into an understandable view of sunlight and Earth visibility. Users click the terrain or enter coordinates, pick a UTC date, and scrub or play a timeline. The app builds a local terrain horizon from NASA LRO LOLA elevation data and compares it with Sun and Earth directions from NASA JPL Horizons. It shows when the Sun and Earth are above the horizon, with a terrain overview and a 360-degree view from the lander. Users can save up to three scenarios to compare sites and dates side by side. This addresses the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge by making power and direct-to-Earth geometry easy to explore without complex tools. It matters because low Sun angles at the pole let nearby terrain block light and Earth, so site and timing choices are linked. The prototype is for education and early concepts, not operational decisions.
details:
What it does. FullSleep Navigator lets a user choose a site on the lunar south pole (by clicking the terrain or entering coordinates) and a UTC date, then move through time with a scrubber or play button. The app updates illumination and Earth visibility, hourly event summaries and the next transition within the loaded analysis window. Two views show the same geometry: a surface overview with local terrain, an elevation layer and a segmented visibility layer, and a view from the lander where the user can rotate 360 degrees, face the Sun or Earth, and see which directions are blocked by the horizon. Up to three scenarios (site, date, observer height, antenna mask) can be saved and compared. Simple solar-power estimates are included. In our example at 89.54 S, 0 E, a window starting 15 Nov has 0 hours of sunlight, while one starting 20 Nov has 70 hours, and Earth is geometrically visible for 87 and 168 hours respectively.

How it works. The terrain comes from NASA PGDA product 90 (LDEM_80S_80MPP_ADJ, adjusted LRO LOLA south-polar DEM, 80 m source spacing), packaged as 513 x 513 grids: a central extent of about 156 m per cell and a regional one of about 1.19 km. Sun and Earth directions come from NASA JPL Horizons (airless apparent azimuth and elevation, 3-hour samples, November 2026), which the browser interpolates. For each site we compute a terrain horizon on a sphere (radius 1,737.4 km, radial search to 300 km) at 2-degree azimuth steps, and 10-degree steps for map cells, then compare it with the Sun and Earth elevations hourly.

Benefits and impact. Lighting and line of sight are the main constraints for south-pole sites. Our tool makes the link between place, date and terrain visible to students, educators and early mission concepts in one browser, with NASA inputs shown openly.

Creativity. The “stand on it” lander view and the three-scenario comparison turn abstract geometry into something users can look around in and compare.

Limitations. This is an approximate exploratory pipeline: November 2026 only, hourly events, object-center visibility, simplified terrain sampling. Earth visibility is a geometric estimate, not a validated radio link. Power estimates are approximate.

Tools. [FILL: front-end stack, e.g. HTML/JavaScript, framework and libraries you used], NASA PGDA and JPL Horizons data, deployed on Vercel. Code and presentation drafting were AI-assisted; the project concept is ours.
